8:["$","$L13",null,{"data":{"chapterId":2,"verseId":10,"chapterTitle":"Examination of Motion","totalVerses":25,"verseData":{"id":"v2_10","number":10,"title":"The Paradox of Inherent Predication","sanskrit":{"text":"","transliteration":"","translation":"For him from whose perspective a mover moves, There would be the consequence that Without motion there could be a mover. Because a mover moves."},"philosophy":{"insight":"If \"a mover moves\" is an inherent fact, then the \"mover\" must be establishable independently of motion (since inherent things are independent). But then a mover could exist WITHOUT motion — contradicting the very statement that motivated the analysis.","madhyamaka":"Garfield: the verse shows the paradox of inherent predication. If you assert \"a mover inherently moves,\" the mover must have independent existence (that's what \"inherent\" means). But independent existence allows the mover to exist without motion, contradicting the original assertion. Kalupahana: this is a prasaṅga (consequentialist reduction) — the opponent's own premise destroys itself.","quantum":"Measurement Back-Action / Observer Effect: The act of measuring one property (e.g., position) disturbs another (momentum). The measurement context CHANGES the system. Similarly, the act of asserting inherent motion changes the logical landscape — it paradoxically creates the possibility of motion-free movers.","bridge":"Both show that the framework of analysis changes what it analyses. Quantum measurement disturbs the system; inherent predication creates paradoxes the predication was meant to avoid. The \"view\" (perspective/measurement) is not neutral — it shapes the outcome.","accessible":"If you insist \"my phone IS a communication device\" (inherently), then the phone must exist as a phone even without communication capability (broken, no signal). But that contradicts calling it a communication device! The inherent label creates its own contradiction.","twoTruths":"Conventionally, motion begins and ends — people start walking and stop. Ultimately, inherent beginning of motion requires a pre-motion state that somehow transitions to motion, which is paradoxical.","commonMisconception":"This is NOT saying things cannot start moving. It shows that an INHERENT beginning of motion (from a truly static state) cannot be coherently established."},"quantumResonance":{"concept":"Measurement Back-Action / Observer Effect","score":87,"strength":"High","explanation":"The act of measurement changes the system. The act of inherent assertion changes the logical consequences. Both show the framework is not neutral.","caveat":"Structural analogy illustrating shared patterns between quantum physics and Madhyamaka analysis. Educational metaphor, not literal equivalence."},"animation":{"geometry":"Self-Undermining Statement","anchor":"A statement \"A MOVER MOVES\" displayed in glowing text. Step 3: If it exists independently, it doesn't DEPEND on motion for its existence. Step 4: Therefore, it could exist without motion. Step 5: But a \"mover\" without motion is a contradiction. The assertion has destroyed itself.","realLifeExample":"Assert: \"A doctor inherently heals.\" This means the doctor exists independently as a doctor. But then they could be a doctor without healing anyone — which contradicts the assertion. The inherent label undermines itself."},{"q":"Whose perspective is being criticized?","a":"The essentialist who takes conventional descriptions (\"a mover moves\") as descriptions of inherent reality. The mistake isn't in using the phrase conventionally but in treating it as revealing independently existing entities and their inherent properties.","realLifeExample":"Saying \"the company makes products\" is fine conventionally. Treating it as if \"the company\" is an inherent entity independent of its products leads to paradoxes — what IS the company without its products?"},{"q":"How does measurement back-action parallel this?","a":"When you measure a particle's position precisely, you disturb its momentum (Heisenberg). The measurement isn't neutral — it changes the system. Similarly, asserting inherent existence isn't a neutral description — it changes the logical consequences, creating the paradox of independent-yet-motion-dependent movers.","realLifeExample":"Asking \"Are you nervous?\" can MAKE someone nervous. The question isn't neutral — it changes the thing it's asking about. Similarly, asserting inherence changes the logical status of what's being described."},{"q":"Is this a formal prasaṅga argument?","a":"Yes. Prasaṅga means \"consequence\" — you accept the opponent's premise and derive an absurd consequence. Premise: \"A mover inherently moves.\" Consequence: The mover exists independently, hence could exist without motion. But a mover without motion is absurd. Conclusion: The premise is false.","realLifeExample":"Assume: \"This restaurant inherently serves good food.\" Consequence: It's a good restaurant even when the food is terrible. That's absurd → the original claim about inherent quality was wrong."},{"q":"Why is the \"perspective\" important?","a":"The verse says \"for HIM from whose perspective\" — it's noting that the paradox arises specifically from the essentialist perspective. From the conventional perspective, \"a mover moves\" is perfectly fine. The problem is philosophical, not linguistic.","realLifeExample":"From a casual perspective, \"the sun rises\" is fine. From an astronomical perspective, it's wrong (Earth rotates). The paradox depends on which framework you're using. Nāgārjuna is criticising the essentialist framework specifically."},{"q":"How does this verse extend the v.7-9 sequence?","a":"V.7: mutual dependence. Together they show inherent motion is incoherent from every angle.","deeper":"The v.7-10 block is the \"positive deconstruction\" — not just showing problems but revealing why the essentialist framework necessarily fails. The measurement isn't neutral — it changes the system, paralleling how asserting inherence changes the logical landscape."},"advanced":{"question":"What is a prasaṅga argument?","options":["A) A direct proof from axioms","B) Accepting the opponent's premise and deriving an absurd consequence to disprove it","C) An appeal to scripture","D) A probabilistic argument"],"correct":"B","explanation":"Prasaṅga (consequence) arguments accept the opponent's assumption, derive contradictory consequences, and conclude the assumption must be false.
